topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Condominium Act, a condominium "unit" is defined as:
choice_a: All portions of the condominium other than the units
choice_b: The entire condominium project, including common elements
choice_c: A portion of the condominium designed and intended for individual ownership and use
choice_d: Only the exterior structure of the building
explanation: The Virginia Condominium Act defines a unit as the portion of the condominium designed and intended for individual ownership and use, distinguishing it from the common elements owned collectively by all unit owners.
source_note: Virginia Condominium Act, Va. Code §55.1-1900 (Definitions), Title 55.1, Chapter 19

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Condominium Act, "common elements" refers to:
choice_a: Only the parking areas of the condominium
choice_b: Only recreational facilities such as a pool or clubhouse
choice_c: Any portion of the property designated for a single unit owner's exclusive use
choice_d: All portions of the condominium other than the units themselves
explanation: Common elements are defined as all portions of the condominium other than the units, and are owned by the unit owners collectively, typically as tenants in common in proportion to their undivided interest.
source_note: Virginia Condominium Act, Va. Code §55.1-1900 (Definitions)

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Condominium Act, a condominium legally comes into existence only:
choice_a: Upon recordation of the condominium instruments (declaration, bylaws, and plats and plans) in accordance with the Act
choice_b: Upon the sale of the first unit to a purchaser
choice_c: Upon the developer obtaining a local business license
choice_d: Upon the unit owners' association holding its first meeting
explanation: A condominium cannot exist under Virginia law except by the recordation of condominium instruments — the declaration, bylaws, and plats and plans — in accordance with the Virginia Condominium Act.
source_note: Virginia Condominium Act, Va. Code §55.1-1900 et seq., Title 55.1, Chapter 19

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Condominium Act, rights conferred on unit owners by the Act:
choice_a: May always be waived by a provision in the declaration
choice_b: Cannot be waived, and the Act's provisions cannot be varied by agreement
choice_c: Apply only to units sold after the year 2020
choice_d: Apply only to the original developer, not to subsequent purchasers
explanation: The Virginia Condominium Act specifically provides that its provisions may not be varied by agreement and that rights it confers may not be waived, protecting unit owners regardless of contrary declaration language.
source_note: Virginia Condominium Act, Va. Code §55.1-1900 et seq., Title 55.1, Chapter 19

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under Virginia's Resale Disclosure Act, when a seller or the seller's agent submits a written request for a resale certificate to a condominium unit owners' association, the association generally must deliver it within:
choice_a: 3 days after the written request
choice_b: 30 days after the written request
choice_c: 14 days after the written request
choice_d: There is no deadline under Virginia law
explanation: The association, its managing agent, or a third party preparing the certificate must deliver the resale certificate within 14 days after a written request from the seller or seller's agent; failure to do so means the certificate is deemed unavailable.
source_note: Virginia Resale Disclosure Act, Va. Code §55.1-2309, Title 55.1, Chapter 23.1

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under Virginia's Resale Disclosure Act, if a purchaser has not been provided the required resale certificate, the purchaser may:
choice_a: Never cancel once the contract has been ratified
choice_b: Only cancel within 24 hours of contract ratification
choice_c: Only cancel with the association's written permission
choice_d: Cancel the resale contract at any time before settlement, without penalty
explanation: If the resale certificate has not been provided, the purchaser may cancel the contract at any time before settlement without penalty, and any earnest money deposit must be promptly returned.
source_note: Virginia Resale Disclosure Act, Va. Code §55.1-2312, Title 55.1, Chapter 23.1

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, the maximum security deposit a landlord may require from a tenant is:
choice_a: Two months' periodic rent
choice_b: One month's rent
choice_c: Three months' rent
choice_d: There is no maximum under Virginia law
explanation: The Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act caps the security deposit a landlord may require at an amount not to exceed two months' periodic rent.
source_note: Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, Va. Code §55.1-1226, Title 55.1, Chapter 12

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, after termination of a tenancy, a landlord must provide an itemized written notice of any deductions and return the remaining security deposit balance within:
choice_a: 10 days after the tenant vacates
choice_b: 45 days after termination of the tenancy or the date the tenant vacates, whichever occurs last
choice_c: 60 days after the tenant vacates
choice_d: There is no required timeframe under Virginia law
explanation: The landlord must provide an itemized written notice of any deductions, together with the remaining deposit balance, within 45 days after the termination date of the tenancy or the date the tenant vacates, whichever is later.
source_note: Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, Va. Code §55.1-1226, Title 55.1, Chapter 12

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, a landlord's access to a dwelling unit to correct a nonemergency condition generally requires:
choice_a: No notice under any circumstances
choice_b: 30 days' written notice in every instance
choice_c: Reasonable advance notice to the tenant, with entry at reasonable times
choice_d: The tenant's presence during entry in every instance
explanation: For nonemergency access, the landlord must give the tenant reasonable advance notice of intent to enter and may enter only at reasonable times.
source_note: Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, Va. Code §55.1-1229, Title 55.1, Chapter 12

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, a landlord is prohibited from:
choice_a: Increasing rent upon lease renewal
choice_b: Requiring payment of a security deposit
choice_c: Requesting references from a prospective tenant
choice_d: Retaliating against a tenant for exercising a legal right, such as filing a good faith complaint with a governmental authority
explanation: The Act prohibits a landlord from retaliating against a tenant — such as by terminating the tenancy or refusing to renew — because the tenant exercised a legal right, such as filing a complaint with a governmental authority.
source_note: Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, Va. Code §55.1-1258 (Retaliatory conduct prohibited), Title 55.1, Chapter 12

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, which of the following is a required disclosure a landlord must make to a tenant?
choice_a: Known mold conditions in the dwelling unit
choice_b: The landlord's personal financial statements
choice_c: The landlord's Social Security number
choice_d: The tenant's credit score
explanation: The Act requires a landlord to disclose known visible evidence of mold in the dwelling unit to a prospective tenant prior to occupancy.
source_note: Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, Va. Code §55.1-1215 (Disclosure of mold in dwelling units), Title 55.1, Chapter 12

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: In Virginia, a person or entity that provides management services to a common interest community, such as a condominium or property owners' association, must generally:
choice_a: Be licensed only if the community has more than 100 units
choice_b: Obtain a license from the Common Interest Community Board, unless exempted
choice_c: Hold only a real estate broker's license, with no additional common interest community requirement
choice_d: Register with the local locality only, with no state licensing requirement
explanation: Virginia requires any person, partnership, corporation, or other entity offering management services to a common interest community to hold a license issued by the Common Interest Community Board, unless a specific exemption applies.
source_note: Virginia Common Interest Community Act, Va. Code §54.1-2346, Title 54.1, Chapter 23.3

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: A licensed Virginia real estate broker whose firm also provides management services to a homeowners' or condominium association should be aware that:
choice_a: A real estate broker's license automatically authorizes common interest community management
choice_b: Common interest community management is entirely unregulated in Virginia
choice_c: Those management services may separately require licensure under the Common Interest Community Board, in addition to the broker's real estate license
choice_d: Only unlicensed assistants may lawfully perform common interest community management
explanation: Providing management services to a common interest community is a separately regulated activity under the Common Interest Community Board, and a real estate broker's license alone does not authorize that activity.
source_note: Virginia Common Interest Community Act, Va. Code §54.1-2345 et seq., Title 54.1, Chapter 23.3

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Virginia's Common Interest Community Board oversees consumer protection mechanisms that include:
choice_a: A state-funded homeowners' insurance pool covering all associations
choice_b: Direct enforcement of each individual association's bylaws by the Board itself
choice_c: Licensing of individual unit owners
choice_d: A Common Interest Community Management Recovery Fund and a Common Interest Community Ombudsman
explanation: The Common Interest Community Board administers a Management Recovery Fund and a Common Interest Community Ombudsman's office to assist consumers with complaints and financial recovery related to community managers.
source_note: Virginia Common Interest Community Act, Va. Code §54.1-2354.3 (Ombudsman) and §54.1-2354.5 (Management Recovery Fund), Title 54.1, Chapter 23.3

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under Virginia's Underground Utility Damage Prevention Act, before beginning excavation or demolition work, a contractor or excavator must:
choice_a: Notify the notification center and observe the required waiting period before digging
choice_b: Notify only the property owner
choice_c: Provide no notice at all if the excavation occurs on private property
choice_d: Notify utilities only if damage to a line is anticipated
explanation: The Act requires anyone planning excavation or demolition to notify the notification center in advance and to observe the statutory waiting period before beginning work, so that underground lines can be located and marked.
source_note: Virginia Underground Utility Damage Prevention Act, Va. Code §56-265.17, Title 56, Chapter 10.3

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Underground Utility Damage Prevention Act, operators of underground utility lines are required to:
choice_a: Perform the excavation work on behalf of the contractor
choice_b: Join a notification center and mark the approximate location of their lines after receiving notice of proposed excavation
choice_c: Respond only to notification requests submitted by government agencies
choice_d: Have no further obligation once a local building permit has been issued
explanation: Operators of underground utility lines must join a notification center and, upon receiving notice of proposed excavation, mark the approximate location of their lines within the statutory timeframe.
source_note: Virginia Underground Utility Damage Prevention Act, Va. Code §56-265.16:1 and §56-265.22, Title 56, Chapter 10.3

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Underground Utility Damage Prevention Act, an operator or excavator who fails to comply with notification requirements and damages an underground utility line may be subject to:
choice_a: No consequence unless a person is physically injured
choice_b: Only an informal verbal warning
choice_c: Civil liability and civil penalties, including penalties that may be imposed by the State Corporation Commission
choice_d: Automatic felony criminal charges in every instance
explanation: The Act provides for civil liability between operators and excavators for damage caused by noncompliance, and authorizes the State Corporation Commission to impose civil penalties for certain violations.
source_note: Virginia Underground Utility Damage Prevention Act, Va. Code §56-265.25 and §56-265.32, Title 56, Chapter 10.3

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Property Owners' Association Act, a lot owners' association generally has authority to:
choice_a: Establish zoning regulations for the surrounding locality
choice_b: Override recorded restrictive covenants at its own discretion
choice_c: Impose criminal penalties on lot owners for rule violations
choice_d: Adopt and enforce rules governing the use of lots and common areas within the development
explanation: The Property Owners' Association Act authorizes an association to adopt and enforce reasonable rules governing the use of lots and common areas, consistent with the recorded declaration and the Act.
source_note: Virginia Property Owners' Association Act, Va. Code §55.1-1819, Title 55.1, Chapter 18

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Property Owners' Association Act, unpaid assessments owed by a lot owner may result in:
choice_a: A lien on the lot in favor of the association, which may be enforced by foreclosure
choice_b: Immediate eviction of the lot owner from the property
choice_c: Automatic transfer of title to the association
choice_d: No recourse available to the association
explanation: The Property Owners' Association Act gives an association a lien on a lot for unpaid assessments, which the association may enforce through foreclosure in the same manner as a mortgage or deed of trust.
source_note: Virginia Property Owners' Association Act, Va. Code §55.1-1833 (Lien for assessments; foreclosure), Title 55.1, Chapter 18

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Property Owners' Association Act, the "statement of lot owner rights" is intended to:
choice_a: Waive a lot owner's right to vote at association meetings
choice_b: Inform lot owners of their basic rights and responsibilities under the Act
choice_c: Serve as a substitute for the recorded declaration
choice_d: Apply only to lots acquired through foreclosure
explanation: The statement of lot owner rights is a plain-language summary designed to inform lot owners of their basic rights and responsibilities under the Property Owners' Association Act; it does not replace the recorded declaration or waive any statutory rights.
source_note: Virginia Property Owners' Association Act, Va. Code §55.1-1807 (Statement of lot owner rights), Title 55.1, Chapter 18

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, which of the following occupancies is expressly excluded from coverage as a "residential tenancy"?
choice_a: A single-family home rented on a month-to-month basis
choice_b: An apartment leased for a fixed one-year term
choice_c: An owner-occupied condominium unit, or a proprietary lease holder's unit in a cooperative
choice_d: A duplex unit rented to a tenant who pays monthly rent
explanation: The Act's definition of "tenancy" excludes several categories of occupancy, including owner-occupied condominium units and proprietary lease holders' units in a cooperative, along with certain institutional, fraternal, transient, and no-rent occupancies.
source_note: Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, Va. Code §55.1-1201(C), Title 55.1, Chapter 12

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, as part of the duty to maintain a fit and habitable dwelling, a landlord must provide the tenant with:
choice_a: A copy of the landlord's homeowner's insurance declarations page
choice_b: A written appraisal of the dwelling unit's market value
choice_c: A list identifying every other tenant in the building
choice_d: A certificate stating that all smoke alarms are present, have been inspected, and are in good working order
explanation: Among the landlord's duties to maintain fit premises, the Act requires the landlord to provide the tenant a certificate confirming that all smoke alarms in the unit are present, have been inspected, and are in good working order.
source_note: Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, Va. Code §55.1-1220, Title 55.1, Chapter 12

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, to terminate a month-to-month tenancy, a landlord or tenant must generally serve written notice on the other party:
choice_a: At least 30 days prior to the next rent due date, unless the rental agreement provides for a different notice period
choice_b: At least 60 days prior to the next rent due date in every instance
choice_c: At least 7 days prior to the next rent due date in every instance
choice_d: No written notice is required to terminate a month-to-month tenancy
explanation: Either the landlord or the tenant may terminate a month-to-month tenancy by serving written notice on the other at least 30 days before the next rent due date, unless the rental agreement specifies a different period.
source_note: Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, Va. Code §55.1-1253, Title 55.1, Chapter 12

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, a tenant who is a victim of family abuse and provides the landlord with a valid protective order may terminate the rental agreement early, with the termination becoming effective:
choice_a: Immediately upon the tenant's oral notice to the landlord
choice_b: 28 days after the tenant serves the termination notice on the landlord, and the landlord may not charge liquidated damages
choice_c: Only at the natural end of the current lease term
choice_d: 90 days after the tenant serves notice, and the landlord may charge a liquidated damages fee
explanation: A tenant who is a victim of family abuse, sexual abuse, criminal sexual assault, or stalking may terminate the rental agreement by serving written notice with a copy of the protective order or conviction order; termination is effective 28 days after the notice is served, and the landlord may not charge liquidated damages.
source_note: Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, Va. Code §55.1-1236, Title 55.1, Chapter 12

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, a landlord's nonrefundable application fee for a rental unit that is not HUD-regulated housing is generally capped at:
choice_a: $500, with no additional expenses permitted
choice_b: An amount equal to one month's rent
choice_c: $50, plus the landlord's actual out-of-pocket expenses for a credit report or background check
choice_d: There is no cap on application fees under Virginia law
explanation: The Act caps a landlord's nonrefundable application fee at $50 (with a lower cap for HUD-regulated housing), plus the landlord's actual out-of-pocket expenses for obtaining a credit report or background check on the applicant.
source_note: Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, Va. Code §55.1-1203, Title 55.1, Chapter 12

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Condominium Act's special provisions for conversion condominiums, an existing tenant who receives the required notice of conversion generally has:
choice_a: No purchase rights of any kind once conversion begins
choice_b: Only 24 hours to decide whether to purchase the unit
choice_c: A purchase right that expires the moment the declaration is recorded
choice_d: An exclusive right to contract to purchase the tenant's own unit for at least 60 days after the notice is given
explanation: The Act's special provisions for conversion condominiums give an existing tenant who receives the required conversion notice an exclusive right to contract to purchase that tenant's unit for at least 60 days after the notice is delivered.
source_note: Virginia Condominium Act, Va. Code §55.1-1982 (Conversion condominiums; special provisions), Title 55.1, Chapter 19

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Condominium Act's special provisions for conversion condominiums, a declarant seeking to terminate a month-to-month tenancy in connection with the conversion must give the tenant:
choice_a: At least 120 days' written notice
choice_b: At least 30 days' written notice, the same as any other month-to-month tenancy
choice_c: No notice, because conversion overrides ordinary tenancy protections
choice_d: At least 10 days' written notice
explanation: Because conversion displaces existing tenants, the Act requires a declarant to give a month-to-month tenant at least 120 days' notice to terminate the tenancy in connection with a conversion condominium, substantially longer than the ordinary 30-day notice.
source_note: Virginia Condominium Act, Va. Code §55.1-1982 (Conversion condominiums; special provisions), Title 55.1, Chapter 19

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Condominium Act, the unit owners' association's executive board must conduct a study to determine the reserves needed for future capital repairs and replacements at least:
choice_a: Once every 20 years
choice_b: Once every five years, with an annual review of the reserve's adequacy
choice_c: Only when a majority of unit owners petition for one
choice_d: Virginia law does not require any reserve study
explanation: The Act requires the executive board to have a reserve study conducted at least once every five years to determine the reserves necessary for capital components, with an annual review of whether the reserve remains adequate.
source_note: Virginia Condominium Act, Va. Code §55.1-1965 (Annual budget; reserve study), Title 55.1, Chapter 19

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Condominium Act, absent a unit-owner-approved extension, a declarant's control of a condominium that is not expandable and has no convertible land must end no later than:
choice_a: Ten years after settlement of the first unit sold
choice_b: Declarant control never automatically ends under Virginia law
choice_c: Two years after settlement of the first unit sold
choice_d: Six months after settlement of the first unit sold
explanation: The Act limits declarant control to two years after settlement of the first unit sold for an ordinary condominium (longer periods of three or five years apply to condominiums with convertible land or expansion rights), and any extension beyond those limits requires a two-thirds vote of the other unit owners, capped at 15 years overall.
source_note: Virginia Condominium Act, Va. Code §55.1-1943 (Control of condominium by declarant), Title 55.1, Chapter 19

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Condominium Act, the unit owners' association is required to maintain property insurance covering the condominium's common elements and structures in an amount:
choice_a: Equal only to the original purchase price of the land
choice_b: Equal to the outstanding balance of unit owners' individual mortgages
choice_c: There is no property insurance requirement under Virginia law
choice_d: Consonant with the full replacement value of the insured property
explanation: The Act requires the unit owners' association to maintain fire and extended coverage insurance on the condominium's insurable common property in an amount consonant with its full replacement value, in addition to master liability coverage and, where assessments are collected, a fidelity bond.
source_note: Virginia Condominium Act, Va. Code §55.1-1963 (Insurance), Title 55.1, Chapter 19

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Common Interest Community Act, a licensed Virginia real estate broker or salesperson who merely sells or leases lots within a common interest community, without providing ongoing management services, is:
choice_a: Exempt from the requirement to hold a separate Common Interest Community Manager license for that sales or leasing activity
choice_b: Required to obtain a Common Interest Community Manager license before listing any lot
choice_c: Prohibited from selling lots located within a common interest community
choice_d: Required to register each such transaction with the Common Interest Community Board before closing
explanation: The Act exempts licensed real estate brokers and salespersons from Common Interest Community Manager licensure for ordinary sales and leasing activity; a separate CIC Manager license is needed only if the broker's firm actually provides ongoing management services to the community.
source_note: Virginia Common Interest Community Act, Va. Code §54.1-2347 (Exemptions), Title 54.1, Chapter 23.3

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Common Interest Community Act, a "common interest community" is defined as real estate subject to a declaration that:
choice_a: Requires every owner within it to be a licensed real estate agent
choice_b: Obligates a lot owner, by virtue of that ownership, to be a member of an association and to pay assessments for common expenses
choice_c: Applies exclusively to time-share projects
choice_d: Applies only to developments containing fewer than 10 lots
explanation: The Act defines a common interest community as real estate subject to a declaration under which a lot owner is, by virtue of ownership, obligated to be a member of an association and to pay assessments of common expenses; time-share projects are specifically excluded from this definition.
source_note: Virginia Common Interest Community Act, Va. Code §54.1-2345 (Definitions), Title 54.1, Chapter 23.3

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under Virginia's Underground Utility Damage Prevention Act, an operator notified of a proposed excavation must mark the approximate horizontal location of its underground line, generally to within two feet of either side, by:
choice_a: Within one hour of the request in every case
choice_b: Within 30 calendar days of the request
choice_c: 7:00 a.m. on the third working day after the request, unless a later date is designated for the excavation
choice_d: There is no deadline for marking underground utility lines
explanation: The Act requires an operator who receives notice of a proposed excavation to mark the approximate horizontal location of its underground line, to within two feet of either side, by 7:00 a.m. on the third working day after the request (or by the scheduled excavation date, if later).
source_note: Virginia Underground Utility Damage Prevention Act, Va. Code §56-265.19, Title 56, Chapter 10.3

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under Virginia's Underground Utility Damage Prevention Act, when an operator receives notice of an emergency excavation, the operator must respond:
choice_a: Within 30 days, the same timeframe as a routine request
choice_b: Only during the operator's regular business hours
choice_c: The Act imposes no emergency response obligation on operators
choice_d: As soon as possible, but no later than three hours after receiving the notice
explanation: For an emergency excavation, the Act requires an operator to respond to the notice as soon as possible, but no later than three hours after receiving it, reflecting the more urgent timeline for emergencies compared with routine excavation requests.
source_note: Virginia Underground Utility Damage Prevention Act, Va. Code §56-265.19, Title 56, Chapter 10.3

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under Virginia's Underground Utility Damage Prevention Act, an "emergency" excavation is one involving:
choice_a: A sudden or unexpected occurrence involving a clear and imminent danger, demanding immediate action to prevent or mitigate loss of, or damage to, life, health, property, or essential public services
choice_b: Any excavation scheduled less than one week in advance
choice_c: Any excavation performed by a homeowner rather than a licensed contractor
choice_d: Any excavation exceeding two feet in depth
explanation: The Act defines "emergency" as a sudden or unexpected occurrence involving a clear and imminent danger demanding immediate action to prevent or mitigate loss of, or damage to, life, health, property, or essential public services, which triggers the Act's expedited three-hour operator response requirement.
source_note: Virginia Underground Utility Damage Prevention Act, Va. Code §56-265.15 (Definitions), Title 56, Chapter 10.3

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under the Virginia Property Owners' Association Act, a lot owner in good standing who wants to examine the association's books and records must generally:
choice_a: Obtain a court order before any records may be examined
choice_b: Give written notice identifying the purpose and records sought at least five business days in advance for a manager-run association, or ten business days for a self-managed association
choice_c: Wait until the association's annual meeting to request records
choice_d: Have no right to examine association records under Virginia law
explanation: The Act gives a lot owner in good standing the right to examine and copy association records upon written notice specifying the purpose and the records requested, given at least five business days in advance for an association with a managing agent, or ten business days for a self-managed association; certain records, such as privileged communications and personnel files, may be withheld.
source_note: Virginia Property Owners' Association Act, Va. Code §55.1-1815 (Books and records), Title 55.1, Chapter 18

topic: Specific Acts Pertaining to Real Estate Practice
question: Under Virginia's Resale Disclosure Act, a resale contract for a lot or unit in a common interest community must disclose to the purchaser that:
choice_a: The seller has no obligation to disclose that the property is part of an association
choice_b: The purchaser may cancel the contract at any time, even after settlement has occurred
choice_c: The purchaser's right to receive the resale certificate and the right to cancel the contract are conclusively waived if not exercised before settlement
choice_d: A resale certificate need not be provided if the association is self-managed
explanation: The Resale Disclosure Act requires the resale contract itself to disclose several things to the purchaser, including that the purchaser's rights to receive the resale certificate and to cancel the contract under the Act are conclusively waived if not exercised before settlement.
source_note: Virginia Resale Disclosure Act, Va. Code §55.1-2308 (Contract disclosures required), Title 55.1, Chapter 23.1
